summary.text: Heirs to the curse Myrtilus laid on the house of Pelops, Atreus and Thyestes killed their half-brother Chrysippus, fought for Mycenae with a golden lamb and a sun that set in the east, and answered each wrong with a worse: Atreus served Thyestes his own sons, and Aegisthus, the son Thyestes fathered on his daughter, cut Atreus down — until Tyndareus brought the sons of Atreus home and the sceptre of Pelops passed to Agamemnon.

chapters.title: The death of Chrysippus
chapters.text: Before they fought each other, the brothers killed a brother. Laius son of Labdacus, in exile from Thebes, found a host in Pelops and, Apollodorus says, fell in love with Pelops' son Chrysippus while teaching him to drive a chariot, and carried him off. In Hyginus, Laius seized the boy, a bastard son of Pelops, at the Nemean games, and Pelops won him back by war — though Hyginus' list of the handsomest youths names Theseus as the thief. Chrysippus came home only to die: spurred on by Hippodamia, Atreus and Thyestes killed their half-brother, and when Pelops laid the blame on her, she killed herself. At Olympia, Pausanias heard instead that she withdrew to Midea because of Pelops' anger over the boy's death, and that the Eleans later brought her bones there at an oracle's bidding.

chapters.title: The golden lamb and the backward sun
chapters.text: The sons of Pelops scattered from Elis, and Sthenelus son of Perseus, who had married their sister Nicippe, gave Atreus and Thyestes Midea to hold. Atreus had vowed Artemis the finest beast his flocks should bear; when a lamb of gold appeared among them he broke the vow, choked it and shut it in a chest — a debt Artemis would still hold against his son at Aulis. But Aerope, his wife, loved Thyestes and gave him the lamb. So when an oracle bade the Mycenaeans take a son of Pelops for king, Thyestes proposed that the throne go to whoever held the golden lamb — and produced it. Then Zeus, through Hermes, offered Atreus a second wager: the kingdom would be his if the sun ran backward. Thyestes agreed, the sun set in the east, and Atreus took the throne and banished his brother. Pausanias saw Thyestes' grave at the place called the Rams, on the road from Mycenae to Argos, topped with a stone ram for the lamb he won through his brother's wife.

chapters.title: The feast of Thyestes
chapters.text: Only later did Atreus learn of the adultery. Apollodorus says he sent a herald offering peace and, when Thyestes came, slaughtered Aglaus, Callileon and Orchomenus, Thyestes' sons by a Naiad, though they had fled to the altar of Zeus; he boiled them and served them to their father, showed him the extremities once he had eaten his fill, and drove him from the land. Hyginus tells of other wrongs: the banished Thyestes sent Atreus' own son, whom he had raised as his, to kill Atreus, who killed the youth believing him his brother's child; then Atreus feigned reconciliation and served Thyestes his two little sons, Tantalus and Plisthenes, and the Sun turned his chariot away. The poets, Pausanias says, sang of that banquet, and Ovid's Pythagoras warns against loading Thyestean tables.
chapters.citation: Apollod. Epit. 2.13; Hyg. Fab. 86, 88, 244; Paus. 2.18.1; Ov. Met. 15.462

chapters.title: Pelopia at Sicyon
chapters.text: Bent on paying Atreus back, Thyestes asked an oracle and heard that a son fathered on his own daughter would avenge him; Apollodorus says only that he obeyed and begot Aegisthus by her. Hyginus names her Pelopia and draws the tale out. Fleeing to King Thesprotus, Thyestes came by night to Sicyon, where she was leading the dances at a sacrifice to Minerva; as she washed the victims' blood from her robe in a stream, he sprang out with his head veiled and forced her, and she hid his sword under the goddess' statue. When famine fell on Mycenae for Atreus' crime, an oracle sent him to fetch Thyestes home; at Thesprotus' court he saw Pelopia, took her for the king's daughter and married her, already carrying her father's child. She exposed the boy she bore; shepherds put him to a she-goat — whence, says Hyginus, his name — and Atreus reared him as his own.

chapters.title: The sword and the return
chapters.text: Hyginus lets the sword finish the tale. Agamemnon and Menelaus seized Thyestes at Delphi, and Atreus sent Aegisthus, the boy he believed his own, to kill him in prison. But Thyestes knew the sword the youth wore; Pelopia, summoned, learned whose it was and drove it into her own breast. Aegisthus carried the bloody blade to Atreus as proof of his brother's death, killed him as he sacrificed on the shore, and brought his father back to the throne. In Apollodorus, the grown Aegisthus learned who his father was, killed Atreus and restored Thyestes; a nurse carried Atreus' young sons to Polyphides of Sicyon, who sent them on to Oeneus in Aetolia, until Tyndareus brought them home. Thyestes, a suppliant at Hera's altar, was bound by oath and sent to Cythera, and Agamemnon, wed to Clytemnestra after killing her first husband, Tantalus the Younger, son of Thyestes, ruled Mycenae.

chapters.title: The sceptre of Pelops
chapters.text: The sceptre Agamemnon held before Troy, Homer says, was Hephaestus' work for Zeus: Zeus gave it to Hermes, Hermes to Pelops the charioteer, Pelops to Atreus; dying, Atreus left it to Thyestes of the many flocks, and Thyestes left it for Agamemnon to bear as lord of many islands and all Argos. By Agamemnon's homecoming the house where Thyestes once lived was the home of Aegisthus, his son. Pausanias found the sceptre worshipped at Chaeronea as the Spear — brought to Phocis, he thought, by Agamemnon's daughter Electra — and at Mycenae saw Atreus' grave and the underground chambers where he and his children had kept their treasure. Whether Aegisthus began the next wrong or Agamemnon, by killing Clytemnestra's first husband, he would not judge; if Pelops' blood-guilt and the vengeful ghost of Myrtilus hounded the family, it only bore out the Pythia's word that punishment passes to a wrongdoer's descendants.
